title: Where should you look for cost savings across a client's business?
description: Where costs hide (value chain) for case interviews. Use with "How to reduce costs?" to find specific levers in each part of the business.
hook: When a client needs to spend less, it helps to have a ready list of the levers they can pull. Here they are, grouped so you can scan them quickly in a case.
body:
When it helps

Use with "How to reduce costs?" to find specific levers in each part of the business.

The checklist

Inputs

  • Renegotiate or switch suppliers
  • Buy in bulk or jointly
  • Redesign the input

Operations

  • Automate
  • Cut waste and rework
  • Make vs outsource

People

  • Flexible staffing
  • Less overtime
  • Fewer management layers

Sales and marketing

  • Cut low-return spend
  • Shift channel mix

Distribution

  • Optimise routes
  • Renegotiate logistics

Overheads

  • Centralise shared services
  • Property, travel

An example

Imagine a regional airline that needs to cut costs by 10%. Walking along the chain: fuel (inputs) through hedging and newer planes; turnaround time on the ground (operations); crew scheduling (people); travel agent commissions (sales); airport fees (distribution); and head office (overheads). Then you ask which of these is biggest. For an airline, fuel and crew usually are, so you start there.

How it sounds in an interview

Let me walk along the business from inputs to customers and list where the cost sits, then focus on the two biggest lines.

Put an amount against every saving idea

Imagine a parcel operator with £100 million of annual costs: £45 million drivers, £30 million transport, £15 million sorting, and £10 million overhead. A vague answer says "automate and negotiate suppliers". A useful answer quantifies a few levers before choosing one.

If route redesign cuts driver hours by 6%, the gross saving is £2.7 million. If reducing empty kilometres cuts transport costs by 4%, that is another £1.2 million. But avoid adding them blindly: better routes might cause both savings, so the effects may overlap. Ask whether the estimates use the same baseline.

Your recommendation should compare annual saving, one-time implementation cost, service impact and time to benefit. A £1 million project that saves £2 million a year may be preferable to an immediate £500,000 cut that increases missed deliveries and customer churn. Always protect the metric the client cannot afford to damage.
outro: The Where costs hide (value chain) checklist is also on the free frameworks page. Next in this topic: How do you use the 3Cs to get started on an open case question?
